blocks.text: datasette-llm is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins.
This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol.
This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0) you can run Datasette via uvx like this:

wget https://datasette.io/content.db

uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \
  --root --secret 1 \
  -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model '{
    "model": "lmstudio-qwen",
    "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b",
    "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1"
  }' content.db
And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model!

About PCAST

The President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) brings together the Nation’s foremost luminaries in science and technology to advise the President and provide recommendations on strengthening American leadership in science and technology.

President Donald J. Trump established PCAST through Executive Order 14177 and appointed the first members of his PCAST in March 2026. PCAST is co-chaired by David Sacks, former Special Advisor for AI & Crypto, and Michael Kratsios, Assistant to the President and Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy.

PCAST may be composed of up to 24 members who are appointed by the President. Individual members serve without compensation and provide leading expertise on emerging technologies such as super intelligence (SI), quantum, nuclear, and biotechnology. PCAST members advise the President on the opportunities and challenges introduced by these technologies to ensure all Americans thrive in this New Golden Age of Science and Innovation. Since President Franklin D. Roosevelt created his Science Advisory Board in 1933, each President has established his own advisory committee of scientists, engineers, and industry leaders.

blocks.text: Airlock
Intent-BasedAccess Control
Airlock is the missing authorization layer for agentic software. Every call an agent makes is evaluated against its intent and then allowed, denied, or sent to a human.
Agents are dynamic. Permissions are static.
Least privilege requires hard-coding permissions. An agent's job is unknown until runtime, so teams settle for one of two extremes.
Manual approval
Safe, until you stop reading the prompts you're approving.
Allow this command?1. Yes   ❯ 2. Always allow  · 3. No
YOLO mode
Fast, until the agent does something you can't undo.
$ agent --dangerously-skip-permissions214 tool calls · 0 reviewed
With Airlock, you don't have to compromise.
Airlock derivespermissions from intent.
No roles to assign, no scopes to pre-grant. Airlock authorizes agent access to all of your tools and integrations.
Intent
The task defines what the agent is allowed to do.
“Find last month's duplicate charges and refund them.”
Actions
The agent calls your tools and integrations as it works.
search · charges, last 30 days
refund · $1,240 in duplicate fees
delete · customer record
Verdicts
Every call is judged against the intent and your rules.
Allowedsearch is read-only
Needs approvalmoves money
Deniedoutside the intent
Write rules in natural language. Enforce them on every request.
Static rules set fixed limits on your integrations. Runtime rules judge what static rules can't.
What should agents be allowed to do?
Agents can read repos, review code, and comment on PRs.
They can merge a PR when CI is passing, it has an approved review, and the change is small in scope.
Anything touching auth, billing, or migrations needs sign-off from the code owner.
Never push to main directly, and never delete branches.
Static Policies
Always in effect
AllowGET
AllowPUT /pulls/*/merge
DenyPOST /git/refs → main
DenyDELETE
Runtime Checks
Judged per call
Check the PR first: CI must pass, has a review, and the diff is small.
Must be less than 200 lines and edit minimal files within a single domain.
Changes touching auth, billing, or migrations must be approved by the code owner.
Run agents securely across your organization.
Use Airlock to manage authorization for all your agents in one place, wherever they run.
Works everywhere
Airlock connects coding agents, custom harnesses, and AI teammates to every tool they need, without changing how they operate.
One set of rules for everyone
Policies live in one place and apply to every agent, on every team. Change a rule once and it takes effect across the organization.
Everything on the record
Every request and every verdict is logged, so security has a complete record of what agents actually do.
Put your agents behind Airlock.
Airlock is available in early access. Request access and tell us what you're building.
Request access

articles.title: Variable Electricity Pricing - the Highs and the Lows
articles.titleZh: Variable Electricity Pricing - the Highs and the Lows
articles.summary: Variable Electricity Pricing - the Highs and the Lows

blocks.text: For one glorious day in September, we had several hours where we were paid to use electricity.

Our home is on Octopus Energy's variable price tariff. Our smart-meter sends back readings every half-hour. That means the energy company can set a different price every half hour. Rather than paying a flat rate of 30p per kWh, we pay a rate which constantly changes throughout the day.
I built a little display out of an old Android tablet. It sits in our kitchen and looks like this:

To be clear, we have chosen this tariff. It is not mandatory. You are free to choose a fixed price tariff if you want. It fits our lifestyle (just about) but we could choose to change back any time we want.

When the sun is shining and the wind a-howling, the UK produces more electricity than it can consume. Our country frequently sells electricity to its neighbours - but it can also sell it to its internal customers. So, for a few hours a day, our meter runs backwards and our electricity bills go down.
That's the happy path. What happens when the skies are cloudy and the wind is still? Prices go up. The other day, we saw this alarming spike:
Yikes! Variable pricing can be unexpectedly high. In Texas a few years ago, a storm caused wholesale prices to rise so much that it caused immediate and long-term financial damage to some people:

The average price for electricity in Texas in the winter is about 12 cents per kilowatt-hour […] Texas utility regulators allowed that price to rise to $9 per kilowatt-hour.
						After Days Of Mass Outages, Some Texas Residents Now Face Huge Electricity Bills
The bill-shock was immense:

For a home that uses 2,000 kWh per month, prices at $9/kWh work out to over $640 per day in energy charges. By comparison, that same household would typically pay $2 per day.
						Griddy Update: Why energy prices were sky high this week
Luckily, Octopus caps the maximum we can pay at £1/kWh. That's still 3x the typical cost, but nowhere near the bankruptcy levels seen in the USA.
How Do We Cope With This?
There are basically two strategies available to minimise our bills.
Electricity Shifting
Demand Shifting

We have a solar array and a big battery. During the day our battery soaks up the sunshine. Because it has an Internet connection, it knows the half-hourly prices - so it discharges at the most expensive times.

That's good enough for watching TV, boiling the kettle, and the like. But the battery doesn't contain enough charge or have enough oomph to run everything like the oven, tumble dryer, and aluminium smelter at once. Which leads us on to demand shifting.

If you saw that evening prices were a quid a kilowatt hour, what behaviours would you change? I put the tumble dryer on early. I made a dinner which didn't require the oven. I read my pre-charged eReader rather than playing on a console.

Did I have to do that? No. I am insulated by the battery - but that won't happen all the time. There will be days when the sun hasn't shone enough to fill up the battery for later. There will be days when I need a hot dinner. There will be days when I want to watch a movie on TV.
Those days will be expensive.
Is This The Future?
I dream of a day when every home has solar panels and a battery. A distributed grid is a resilient grid.

Until then, I don't think a variable tariff is useful for most people. I suspect that the average person doesn't want to delay dinner by an hour just to save £3.14, or to needlessly hoover the house because they'll earn 71p for it.

This is a fun experiment for us. The occasional surge price isn't going to bankrupt us, and we don't have complex needs which mean restricting our energy usage would be catastrophic. But it is easy to see how the lack of predictability could seriously inconvenience someone or cause them needless distress.

I broadly think that people should be more aware of their energy usage. A little bit of behavioural change among many people can lead to a significant positive impact. But I'm also grateful for the £1 cap!
If you'd like to try a variable electricity tariff, join Octopus and we both get £50.

blocks.text: Figuring out when an item was made can be difficult. Sometimes there will be date codes on some of the parts inside, but not always. My friend Andrew Tolch reminded me recently that if you have the box it came in, there may be some very good clues hiding there.

Sometimes, but not always, there will be a date code on the box itself stating when the box was printed. I have one such example, where the date couldn’t be much more clear. The box literally states 09/ 77. That is very common nomenclature for the 9th month of 1977.

Sometimes it’s a bit more subtle than that. He showed me a tin lithographed fire truck made by Marx with the box. Next to the manufacturer’s seal, there was the number 56. That sounds like 1956. And that is well within the time frame either of us would have expected, since the truck was made of lithographed tinplate and also had some plastic components. That mixture of technology was still common in the mid-1950s.

But he pointed out another detail. There were five stars near the number 56. That’s the indicator of the month the box was printed. Five stars means five, for the fifth month of the year, which is May. So the box was printed in May 1956. That means the toy that went in the box was manufactured very close to that date as well. They probably did order boxes somewhat in advance, but a box from the middle of the year probably means the toy came from the middle of the year as well.
So if you have the box the item came in, check the underside of the box, especially if it’s bleached or unbleached cardboard and not with full color printing on all six sides.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.
